what_it_does: Modern processors speed things up by speculatively executing instructions before they know for sure those instructions will be needed — if the guess is wrong, the results are thrown away. Spectre attacks exploit the fact that even discarded speculative work leaves behind traces in the CPU's cache that an attacker can read, leaking secrets. Hardware designers have proposed mitigations, but verifying that a chip's actual low-level hardware description (called RTL, the register-transfer level blueprint used to manufacture chips) truly prevents all leaks has been an unsolved problem. This paper introduces Contract Shadow Logic: extra tracking circuitry that is attached to the chip's RTL blueprint and encodes a formal security contract — a mathematical statement of exactly what information the speculative parts of the processor are allowed to expose. Automated formal verification tools (model checkers) then confirm that no possible execution sequence violates the contract, providing a machine-checked proof of security for the actual hardware design rather than just a high-level argument.
